paragraphs.text: MEHMO syndrome is a rare X-linked intellectual disability syndrome whose name stands for its cardinal features: mental retardation, epileptic seizures, hypogonadism and hypogenitalism, microcephaly, and obesity (Steinmüller et al., 1998; Skopkova et al., 2017). Affected males can also have early-onset insulin-dependent diabetes, growth retardation, and typical facial dysmorphism, and life expectancy may be short (Steinmüller et al., 1998; Skopkova et al., 2017). The syndrome results from mutations in EIF2S3, which encodes the gamma subunit of translation initiation factor eIF2. Missense mutations give a milder phenotype that shows only some of the features (Skopkova et al., 2017; Gregory et al., 2019).

paragraphs.text: Delozier-Blanchet et al. (1989) described 2 brothers with a severe syndrome of postnatal growth and mental retardation. Features included extreme microcephaly, obesity that developed during infancy, microgonadism, and a characteristic amphora-shaped face. The neurologic examination was highly abnormal, with hypertonia, hyperreflexia, nystagmus, and extremely irritable and agitated behavior. The first child died at 4.5 years of age and had also had neonatal hypoglycemia and chronic constipation. The authors noted that the brothers most resembled patients with Börjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome, but their dwarfism and mental retardation were much more severe, and the authors considered either autosomal or X-linked recessive inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Skopkova et al. (2017) studied 4 families with MEHMO syndrome. The index patient in family 1 was born to nonconsanguineous Slovak parents. Microcephaly was diagnosed prenatally at 28 weeks' gestation, and micropenis, cryptorchidism, and peripheral hypertonia were noted at birth. He had partial complex seizures from 4 months of age that resisted anticonvulsants, severe mental and motor delay, central obesity, and dysmorphic features. These included full cheeks, large ears, downturned corners of the mouth, epiblepharon, tapered fingers, and talipes. Non-autoimmune diabetes mellitus was diagnosed at 10 months of age and treated with insulin. Brain MRI showed delayed myelination and, at 19 months, acute demyelinating changes and cerebral atrophy. During intercurrent infections his seizures worsened and his diabetes control deteriorated. Muscle biopsy showed abnormal mitochondria and decreased complex II activity with normal complex IV activity. At 5 years his height was 88 cm (-5 SD) and his head circumference 39 cm (-8.4 SD).

Family 3 was the family originally reported by Steinmüller et al. (1998). Its index patient was diagnosed prenatally with microcephaly. He had therapy-resistant seizures from 7 weeks of age, and diabetes was diagnosed at 6 months during a ketoacidotic crisis. He had permanent seizures toward the end of his life at 2 years. Female mutation carriers in family 3 were unaffected. The proband of family 4 was born to nonconsanguineous parents of Northern European origin living in the US. He had microcephaly, hypospadias and cryptorchidism, developmental delay, and obesity, but no epileptic seizures, and his EEG was normal.

paragraphs.text: Gregory et al. (2019) reported 3 affected males from a nonconsanguineous white European pedigree: monozygotic twin brothers and their maternal cousin. They had severe recurrent hypoglycemia, short stature with growth hormone and TSH deficiencies, and an unusual form of glucose dysregulation that alternated between hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia and postprandial hyperglycemia. Brain MRI showed variable white matter loss and a small anterior pituitary. The twins had a microphallus, and in 1 twin the testes were small and undescended but descended spontaneously by 2 years of age. Both twins nevertheless went through puberty spontaneously. The boys did not have severe intellectual disability or microcephaly, and all attended mainstream school. The authors noted that the boys lacked the microcephaly, epilepsy, and obesity typical of previously reported MEHMO patients.

paragraphs.text: In affected males from 3 families with MEHMO syndrome, 2 from Slovakia and the family originally reported by Steinmüller et al. (1998), Skopkova et al. (2017) identified a hemizygous 4-bp deletion (c.1394_1397delTCAA) in the last exon of the EIF2S3 gene. The deletion was predicted to cause a frameshift and premature stop (Ile465SerfsTer4) that replaces the last 8 amino acids with 3 different residues. It cosegregated with the disease, was absent from dbSNP147 and ExAC, and had a CADD score of 35. The truncated protein was detected in patient fibroblasts, which also showed increased DDIT3 and CHOP levels. In a yeast/human chimeric eIF2-gamma, the mutation caused slow growth, derepressed GCN4 expression, and increased UUG initiation.

agent.process_note: I read all 8 files in full. Three of them, Borck 2012, Skopkova 2017 and Gregory 2019, have full text. Four have only an abstract (Delozier-Blanchet 1989, Steinmüller 1998, Leshinsky-Silver 2002 and Moortgat 2016), and DeLozier-Blanchet 1999 has only a title. I checked variant names, nucleotide changes, zygosity, family numbers and ancestry against the text. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so the intro gives no MIM number for EIF2S3. The chromosome location, Xp22.11, comes from Gregory et al. (2019). The Moortgat abstract does not say which family carried which mutation or what the family origins were, so those details are left out. Skopkova et al. say Steinmüller mapped the locus to Xp11.3-22.13, but the Steinmüller abstract says Xp21.1-p22.13; I used the abstract. Ser108Arg (which its authors classified as a variant of unknown significance) and Val151Leu (which Borck mentions only as a previously reported variant with no phenotype data) were not entered as allelic variants. Ser108Arg is described in Molecular Genetics; Val151Leu is not covered.
